thread.title: What happens when consumers want you to pay for their data?

title: What happens when consumers want you to pay for their data?
text: Managing Director, IBM Global Consumer Electronics Industry, Strategy & Business Development. Business Models & Global Expansion Oct 8 Designing for customer and user experience means device, software and data — from the ground up What happens when consumers want you to pay for their data? Just because you made their device, doesn’t mean you have the right, right? Pretty soon, consumers are going to ask you to pay for their data. It’s not just a reaction to them wanting you to remove the ads that supplement someone’s revenue. It’s not GDPR. It’s simple. If you’re intending to create a revenue stream from what you know or can infer or predict, they are going to want a cut of those dollars, a discount or something in exchange. This is not exactly a new idea. In a 2004 article, the Harvard Business Review put this as a big idea but it was only recently that the balance of power shifted sufficiently for this to be a practicality. Individuals and businesses have long tussled over who owns consumers’ personal data. The decisive blow may be struck by customer-managed interaction (CMI) , a new service model whose implementation is on the horizon. Superficially, CMI declares consumers victorious by ceding them total control over information about their past purchases and product preferences. But it also helps companies harvest the deep consumer knowledge that customer relationship management (CRM) only promises. (1) As consumers become more engaged with managing their digital selves as well as the footprints they leave, electronics companies will need to adjust their data collection and management processes, as well as their payment and revenue share models as well. However, it’s not just consumers looking for a cut. New EU rules on content and copyrights might change the access and display of content. (2) “Where ‘Content’ is King, ‘Service’ is Queen, ‘Devices’ are Wild “ So what exactly is the common ground between consumers and electronics companies in the next three years? Electronics executives must ask “What business am I in ?” as they transform from a dedicated discrete device manufacturer to hybrid device and service provider of sorts. A company can tap into the real needs of their customer to provide “experience based device innovation,” where expansions in capabilities are targeted based on the specific group of services and usage patterns a customer has. It’s estimated that consumers use 30 apps monthly and 10 each day (3), primarily social media apps. However, these rules don’t hold for business centric devices — such as tablet used during work or in the field. In those cases, connected devices must provide specific, relevant information that increasingly examines and combines multiple sources of content for increased context and applicability. Future devices will focus on “Interoperable Innovation” to win consumer favor Privacy versus Ownership — the thin paid line In today’s environment, users fully recognize the “interconnectedness” of the devices they own. Devices connect and share content and data individually and among myriad of service and device combinations. These connected devices are pretty much a part of today’s fabric. Now that the data flowing to and from individual devices within ecosystems is known, the burning issue is who owns, maintains and realizes revenue on the data? And how will this come about? It used to seem like millennials were laissez faire about their privacy, but the truth is closer to them having little expectation of privacy as opposed to anything else. And now, as the world’s major economies leave many millennials unemployed or underemployed, turning their data streams into revenue streams seems like a well deserved stipend for years of driving the internet economy forward. Millennials are the largest labor force in some economies and they have the lowest labor force participation. The joke about do you want fries with that feels snarky to some of us. However, for many millennials, who are in jobs that pay below their potential, and carrying student loans that represent an irrational share of their income, the thought of getting paid for their data makes sense (and dollars). Consumers increasingly want a two sided business model where they’re continuous beneficiaries. The first real life examples are already there — Shiru Cafe near Brown University in Providence, RI, already lets students use their personal data to pay for coffee (4). With calls for privacy and transparency, GDPR has become a ‘flashlight’ on the issues at hand. The backlash in all this with social media and concerns over ‘evil tech’ have hit a boiling point with regulators. Most regulators aren’t especially tech savvy and they struggle to understand tech’s unique relationships with the supply chain and consumers at large. Many countries are considering additional regulations and more fines. Here’s a 10 year snapshot on some of the biggest:(5) December, 2009 —  Microsoft is ordered by the Commission to allow Windows users and computer manufacturers to turn off Internet Explorer and use other browsers. May, 2009 —  Intel ( INTC ) is fined €1.06 billion ($1.2 billion) for abusing its dominant position by paying computer makers to delay or even cancel releases of products that contain chips made by rival AMD. December, 2012 — The Commission fines Philips ( PHG ), LG Electronics , Panasonic ( PCRFF ) and other companies a total of €1.47 billion ($1.7 billion) for running two cartels. March, 2013 —  Microsoft is fined €561 million ($653 million) for not complying with the 2009 Internet Explorer ruling. May, 2014 — Europe’s top court rules that people have the right to be forgotten and search engines like Google must remove certain unwanted links. August, 2016 — The Commission orders Ireland to recover up to €13 billion ($14.6 billion) in unpaid taxes from Apple ( AAPL ). May, 2017 —  Facebook ( FB ) is fined €110 million ($122 million) for misleading European officials about its takeover of messaging service WhatsApp. June, 2017 —  Google ( GOOGL ) is fined a record €2.4 billion ($2.7 billion) for using its search engine to steer internet users towards its own shopping platform. October, 2017 — The Commission orders Amazon ( AMZN ) pay unpaid taxes of €250 million ($293 million) after finding that it benefited from an illegal arrangement with Luxembourg. January, 2018 — The Commission fines Qualcomm ( QCOM ) €997 million ($1.2 billion) for paying billions to Apple not to use chips made by competitors. March, 2018 — Europe tells tech companies including Google, Facebook and Twitter ( TWTR ) to take down terrorist content within an hour of it being flagged or face new legislation and fines. May, 2018 — Europe’s new data protection law, the General Data Protection Regulation, comes into effect, setting up new strict rules for how companies handle personal data. July, 2018 —  Google is hit with a new record €4.34 billion ($5 billion) fine over Android. Trust and Transparency aren’t optional Complexity, industry convergence and device interoperability have all been elusive, and this has raised trust and transparency to a higher order demand. Consumers and companies are no longer willing to accept “black box” approaches to how their devices work or how they operate in a larger context. The electronics industry is spawning products that are more complex to use, difficult to manage, rife with security and privacy concerns. Again, no one device is the star of the show: its all context dependent. Devices are evolving to be ‘social’ much like we humans; they connect, friend and share data across a wide array of services and capabilities, in a multi sided business model. These “socialized” devices often act as IoT agents, connecting, friending, sharing with manufacturers, and service ecosystems as well as across other devices for the consumers’ lifestyle experiences …to create new experiences among and between new services. While each manufacturer dreams of getting closer to customers, the reality is more of an interoperability nightmare. For many of those who put effort into developing direct intimate customer relationships, there hasn’t been the desired payout and consumers are still seeking the “one ring” to hold all their potential IoT relationships. Consumer/User experience is the disruptive force The fundamental driving force behind all the disruption is the evolving customer experience*, and everything else follows from that. So what do executives in the Electronics Industry need to know and do? Keep these three things in mind, and you’re off to a good start. *most of the time “consumer” is used as the operative term for any user. We also want to make it clear instead of adding complexity every time, consumer in this case reflects the B2B side of our industry as well, using the term interchangeably. Don’t confuse the device as the product. The device is no longer the star of the show. AI embedded in a device enables user experience differentiation. However, it can also obscure the underlying hardware or product differentiation, requiring companies to find new ways to pursue value. Cloud-based AI platforms have enabled ecosystems that have the capability to completely disintermediate manufacturers. If differentiation is brought about by the ecosystem, electronics companies must find new ways to differentiate their products with services. Trust, transparency, and avoidance of bias are key. As ecosystems share data from increasing numbers of sources, it becomes ever more critical that the consumers trust the ecosystem. “Possessing the data” may not be sufficient, and using it is expected to evolve to a permissions-based approach that balances control and access, e.g., with emerging personal data stores. Companies need to understand data provenance and usage rules across their ecosystem. In many cases, there is little transparency, shared data, algorithms, and obscure ownership. Product is still the face of the ecosystem. In many cases, the device manufacturer is the one that stands to lose the most when things go awry; Most consumers can’t tell which part of their experience is delivered by which company in the ecosystem, and the brand that is visible on the device they hold in their hand often gets the blame, whether they were the culprit or not. Device companies need to choose their ecosystem partners carefully. Reach out to the author, Scott Burnett Read more of Scott’s perspectives on Digital Reinvention
